newsitem.title: USA: Arizona gov. accused of fraud says audit was unnecessary.
newsitem.headline: Arizona gov. accused of fraud says audit was unnecessary.

text.p: Arizona Gov. Fife Symington said Wednesday that he shunned full-blown audits of his books during his days as a developer, concerned that it could plunge him into serious trouble.
Symington testified in his federal fraud trial that he wanted to assign the values for his real estate properties in the mid-1980s because he had a better idea of their worth.

Saying such an audit was "totally unnecessary," Symington said at the time that any calculations from his accountants Coopers & Lybrand could throw him into default on guarantees he made to a Japanese bank to fund a large development.
The two-term governor testified under cross-examination by prosecutor David Schindler that he only had the firm check the "methodology and consistency" of the statements.

Symington, who jousted with Schindler several times during the day-long testimony, is charged with 22 counts of fraud, attempted extortion and perjury. If convicted on a single count, he would be removed from office and could go to prison.

The prosecution continued Wednesday to try to show that the Republican governor changed his story on papers given to various financial institutions to get loans or seek concessions. In some cases, his bottom line changed dramatically depending on what he sought, prosecutors allege.

Additionally, they claim he tried to extort loan concessions from union pension funds and lied under oath in bankruptcy proceedings. He filed for Chapter 7, which sets liquidation into motion, in 1995.

Symington, 51, has continued to maintain his innocence, saying he made mistakes but committed no fraud. He also has said that his accountants should have caught many of the missteps that were made in his financial statements.
Earlier Wednesday, the judge presiding over the trial admonished the jury about discussing the case outside of court.

Judge Roger Strand issued the warning after becoming aware of allegations that two jurors were overheard discussing Symington's taxes as they exited U.S. District Court in Phoenix. His taxes were mentioned in court Tuesday.
"It is not anything the court intends to pursue," Strand told jurors, adding that the details of Tuesday's incident were sketchy and that they were anonymous.
Attorneys from both sides said they did not believe that the incident -- one of several that have occurred during the 12-week-trial -- was cause for a mistrial.

But it did prompt The Associated Press to temporarily pull off the reporter who has covered the trial. Reporter Jerry Nachtigal was the person who witnessed the conversation and reported it later that day.
"We were concerned that he might be called as a witness about what he heard," said Sue Cross, the wire service's bureau chief in Phoenix.
